scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

The person is a senior in high school, female, with a younger sister in grade 10. Schools have been closed for a while and won't reopen for at least another month. Their dad works from home, but their mom still goes to her office. The school just started online teaching, and they've been getting a lot of assignments. The mom expects them to make dinner every night because "we're home all day." The person got upset because even though they're home, they have schoolwork to do. She asked her mom why she doesn't cook since she finishes work at 5 pm and her office is only 6 minutes away. The mom got angry when she came home and saw no dinner, and she started screaming about being ashamed and how they're useless. The person explained that being home all day doesn't mean they have the whole day off, and the mom said it doesn't take that long to cook. The person retorted by asking why the mom doesn't cook then.

From the context, the mom is an awful cook, doesn't put effort into learning or looking up recipes. The dad is an excellent cook but has a high-demand job, coming home as late as 9 or 10 pm. He often ends up making dinner late or eating fast food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be ready. The dad also offers to cook for the girls if their mom didn't make a proper meal. The person is a good cook too and has been doing a lot of cooking during the first few weeks before online school started, including baking treats. The dad does practically all the chores, while the mom spends her time watching TV.

The question is: AITA (Am I The Asshole) for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, the dad ended up cooking in the end today.

So, the main points are:

1. The person and her sister are home all day but have schoolwork to do.
2. The mom expects them to cook dinner every night.
3. The mom is a bad cook and doesn't contribute much.
4. The dad is the primary cook but has a demanding job.
5. The person is a good cook but has been handling schoolwork.
6. The person refused to cook today, leading to an argument with the mom.
7. The dad ended up cooking.

Now, I need to evaluate whether the person's action is morally acceptable or not.

First, let's consider the expectations. The mom expects the kids to cook dinner every night because they're home all day. However, the kids have schoolwork to do, which is a valid responsibility. It's reasonable for them to prioritize their schoolwork, especially since online school has just started and they have a lot of assignments.

The mom's expectation might be unrealistic because she doesn't account for the kids' responsibilities. She also doesn't contribute much to cooking or chores, which adds to the burden on the kids and the dad.

The person's refusal to cook today was because she had schoolwork to do. She also pointed out that the mom could cook since she finishes work early. However, the mom is a bad cook and doesn't put effort into it, which the person knows. So, the person's frustration is understandable.

The argument escalated when the mom got angry and started screaming, which is not a constructive way to handle the situation. The person stood her ground, which might be seen as standing up for herself, but the way she did it could be seen as confrontational.

In the end, the dad cooked, which is a common occurrence. The dad is already overburdened with his job and chores, so adding more cooking to his plate isn't fair either.

So, considering all this, is the person's action morally acceptable?

On one hand, the person has valid reasons for not cooking: schoolwork and the mom's lack of contribution. On the other hand, refusing to cook and confronting the mom in that way might be seen as disrespectful or uncooperative, especially since the mom is trying to manage the household.

However, the mom's behavior of expecting the kids to cook without considering their responsibilities and not contributing herself is also problematic. The person's frustration is justified, but the way she expressed it might not be the best approach.

In terms of morality, the person's refusal to cook due to schoolwork is understandable, but the confrontation might be seen as unacceptable. However, considering the context of the mom's behavior and the unfair expectations, the person's action might be seen as a form of self-defense or standing up for her rights.

Therefore, I think the action is morally acceptable because the person had valid reasons for not cooking and was standing up for herself against unreasonable expectations. However, the way she handled the confrontation could be improved, but it doesn't necessarily make the action morally unacceptable.
